blocks.text: Every hash map solution is the same bargain: **spend memory to buy time**. It is worth understanding the exchange rate, because it is not always a good deal.

blocks.code:
brute force:   O(N^2) time,  O(1) space
hash map:      O(N)   time,  O(N) space

blocks.text: For a million elements, the brute force does a trillion operations. The map does a million, and holds a million entries — perhaps 50 MB. Almost always worth it.

items: **The array is already sorted.** Two pointers gives O(N) time and O(1) space — strictly better. Do not reach for a map out of habit.
**Memory is genuinely tight.** Embedded systems, or arrays too large for RAM.
**N is small.** Below a few dozen elements, a nested loop may beat a map's hashing overhead. Big-O describes growth, not small cases.

blocks.text: Hash maps have poor **cache locality**. Entries are scattered across memory by design, so lookups often miss cache — while a linear scan of an array reads sequentially and is very cache-friendly.

This is why an O(N) scan of a small array can genuinely outrun an O(1) map lookup. The constant factors differ by more than people expect. Asymptotics decide large inputs; measurement decides small ones.
If you only need to know *whether* you have seen something, use a **Set**. If you also need *where* or *how many*, use a **Map** with the index or count as the value.

blocks.code:
const seen = new Set();          // membership only
const indexOf = new Map();       // value -> index
const counts = new Map();        // value -> how many times

blocks.text: Those three cover the overwhelming majority of hash-based solutions. Choosing correctly makes the code read as its own explanation.
